failure_summary.description: The answer used an associated or overly specific entity instead of the requested type, scope, or time period despite existing slot and category guidance.
A leading ellipsis was treated as part of the clue rather than a signal to recover the omitted beginning of a phrase.
The correct place was identified, but a jurisdictional qualifier present in the directly paired answer was omitted.
One bare-list prompt was underdetermined from its wording, and one factual claim was answered without reliable supporting evidence.

patch.reasoning: Existing guidance already covers answer type, relation, and scope, so repeating a general slot-check rule would not address the ignored distinctions. Add narrow rules for recovering a missing prefix, choosing an explicitly identified original-language title, and preserving qualifiers when a source directly pairs the clue with a full answer. The ambiguous list and unsupported historical claim do not support a safe general rule.

edits.target: For proper names and titles, use the conventional form that identifies the requested entity. Do not substitute a nickname or later brand name for the historically relevant label, omit words from a work's title when the work is requested, or add optional middle names. Conversely, when the clue requests a generic class, do not embellish it with a narrower associated name.
edits.content: When a work appears under both an original-language title and a translated or market title, prefer the title explicitly identified as the original when the question asks for the work without specifying a release-language title. Use the translation when the clue specifically asks for the English title or release title.

edits.target: In noisy or search-style context, a passage may repeat the clue without supplying its answer. Treat that echo as a locator for relevant material, not as evidence for the missing answer; use substantive passages to identify the target and verify distinctive clue details. If the passage explicitly pairs the clue with an answer, it can serve as direct evidence.
edits.content:
In noisy or search-style context, a passage may repeat the clue without supplying its answer. Treat that echo as a locator for relevant material, not as evidence for the missing answer; use substantive passages to identify the target and verify distinctive clue details. If the passage explicitly pairs the clue with an answer, it can serve as direct evidence; preserve the complete answer label and its supplied qualifiers rather than shortening it just because the referent is clear.

When a quoted fragment begins with an ellipsis, consider whether it signals omitted preceding words. If context identifies the phrase, return the missing prefix—not the visible tail or a work associated with that tail.

edits.target: When a work appears under both an original-language title and a translated or market title, prefer the title explicitly identified as the original when the question asks for the work without specifying a release-language title. Use the translation when the clue specifically asks for the English title or release title.
edits.content: For ellipsis fragments, apply the completion rule only when the ellipsis marks missing text; do not treat a trailing or purely stylistic ellipsis as a blank.
